title: Frances of Rome (9 March)
hookLine: a wife and mother in Rome who cared for the sick in plague years

lines: ONE VERSE, STARTED AGAIN AND AGAIN.
cards: A woman sits down with her prayer book in a big Roman house and opens to the psalm for the hour. She reads the first line. A servant calls with a question.
She marks the place, goes, comes back, reads the same line. Her husband needs her. Then a child.
Then a guest. Tradition says she was called away from that one verse again and again, and every time she went without complaint.
When she finally came back for good, the story goes, the verse on the page was written in gold. This is Frances of Rome.

teach.h: SHE WANTED THE CONVENT, AND GOT A MARRIAGE.
teach.b: Frances, tradition says, wanted from girlhood to enter a convent. Her family arranged a marriage instead, to a young nobleman named Lorenzo Ponziani. She was miserable at first.
Then, with her sister-in-law Vannozza, she found her way: the two of them, in their fine clothes, slipping out to visit the sick and the poor of the city.
The marriage became a long and loving one, and she raised her children in it. Then came hard years for Rome: war, famine and plague.

teach.h: PLAGUE YEARS: THE HOUSE BECOMES CARE.
teach.b: Frances turned the family house into a place of care, gave away the household's grain and wine, nursed the sick, and, tradition says, buried one of her own children in the plague.
A mother in mourning, still out in the streets.

teach.h: LEAVE GOD AT THE ALTAR, FIND HIM AT HOME.
teach.b: A saying handed down from her, often put this way, sums her up: a married woman must sometimes leave God at the altar to find him in her housekeeping. That's the gold verse in a sentence.

Prayer never mattered less to her; serving was prayer by other means. In the Douay-Rheims, Proverbs describes a valiant woman: "She hath opened her hand to the needy, and stretched out her hands to the poor."
Later, Frances gathered women who lived that way without full vows, and after her husband died she joined them.

teach.h: AN ANGEL TO LIGHT THE WAY.
teach.b: Tradition also says she saw her guardian angel at her side, lighting her way at night, which is why she's a patron of drivers.

teach.h: SHE HATH OPENED HER HAND TO THE NEEDY.
teach.b: Her holiness ran through the house, not around it.

how: Catholics keep 9 March as the optional memorial of Saint Frances of Rome; in Rome her body is venerated at the church of Santa Francesca Romana in the Forum, and in some places cars are blessed on her feast because she is patron of drivers.

o: Proverbs' phrase for a strong, generous wife
a title for a woman knighted for bravery
a nun who defends her convent in war

games.q: Frances of Rome — tap the pairs.
p: her sister-in-law and partner in care
after she was called away again and again

s: Frances of Rome was a nun all her life
she was a wife and mother; she joined the community she founded only after her husband died.
she turned her family's house into a place of care
in years of famine and plague she gave away grain and wine and nursed the sick.
Frances thought serving mattered more than prayer
for her, serving was prayer by other means: leave God at the altar to find him at home.

games.q: you're Frances, halfway through the first line of your prayers. a servant calls you away yet again. what do you do?
o: finish the psalm first, then go.
go, without complaint, and come back to the line.
ask not to be disturbed during prayer.
games.why: tradition says she went every time, and when she returned the verse was written in gold.

practice: Picture the people under your roof, or the ones you'd call home if you live alone, and find one small need of theirs you've been stepping around: a dish, a question, a few minutes of listening.
Picture putting down whatever you're doing and going to them, the way Frances closed the book. If you pray, offer that small errand as your prayer; if you don't, just breathe.

wordCard.voice: Valiant woman, the Book of Proverbs' phrase for Frances of Rome: a Roman wife and mother who nursed the sick in plague years and left her prayers, again and again, to serve.

carryVoice: Your line: she left prayer to serve. The verse in gold waited for her. Until tomorrow.
